blocks.text: 1. Introduction

Picture a spreadsheet of orders with a thousand rows, one column for region, one for the amount spent. Someone asks you: "what is the average order size in each region?" You could write a for loop that checks every row, buckets it by region, and keeps a running total. It would work. It would also be slow, clunky, and about ten lines longer than it needs to be. This is exactly the problem groupby() was built to solve, and it does it in one line.

df.groupby() is one of the single most powerful and most used tools in all of pandas. Once it clicks, you will reach for it constantly: total sales per product, average rating per user, count of errors per day, max temperature per city. Almost any question that starts with "for each X, what is..." is a groupby question.

items: A teacher averaging test scores for each class instead of each student.
A spreadsheet pivot table that totals expenses by category.
An inbox that groups emails by sender so you see one thread per person, not one row per email.
A sports league table that sums wins and losses for each team across a whole season.

blocks.text: Every one of those examples follows the exact same three step pattern, and that pattern is the key to understanding literally everything groupby does. It is called split-apply-combine, and the whole rest of this lesson is really just that one idea applied over and over in different shapes.

blocks.caption: The whole lesson in one picture: split, apply, combine.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267410-758526371.png

There is also a real performance reason to prefer groupby over a manual loop. Pandas pushes the grouping and aggregation work down into fast, vectorized, compiled code instead of looping through rows one at a time in plain Python. On anything beyond a tiny toy dataset, that difference is not subtle.
2. The Split-Apply-Combine Mental Model

Every single groupby call, no matter how simple or how complicated it looks, breaks down into exactly three steps. Once you can name the three steps for a piece of code, you understand what that code does, even if you have never seen that exact combination of methods before.
2.1 Split: Breaking the DataFrame into Groups

The split step takes your DataFrame and divides it into smaller pieces, one piece per unique value in the column you grouped by. If you group orders by region and there are three regions in the data, North, South, and East, pandas quietly builds three separate mini DataFrames behind the scenes, one holding every North row, one holding every South row, one holding every East row.

blocks.alt: Split: Breaking the DataFrame into Groups
blocks.caption: Split divides one DataFrame into several smaller ones, grouped by region.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267411-423229073.png
2.2 Apply: Running a Function on Each Group

The apply step runs some function independently on each of those smaller pieces. That function has no idea the other groups even exist. It just sees the rows for North, does its job, for example computing a mean, and hands back one answer for North. Then the exact same function runs again on South, completely separately, and again on East.

blocks.alt: Apply: Running a Function on Each Group
blocks.caption: Apply runs the same function on each group in isolation, one group at a time.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267411-80189792.png
2.3 Combine: Merging Results Back Together

The combine step glues all those separate little answers back into a single object you can actually work with, usually a Series or a DataFrame, indexed by the group keys. North's mean, South's mean, and East's mean stop being three isolated numbers floating around and become one tidy result you can print, plot, or save.

blocks.caption: Combine stitches the per group answers back into a single output.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267411-648853048.png

blocks.title: The three steps always happen
blocks.content: You almost never see split, apply, and combine spelled out as three separate lines of code. Pandas hides them behind one chained call like df.groupby("region")["total"].mean(). But all three steps are still happening under the hood, every single time. When a groupby line confuses you, slow down and ask what got split, what function got applied, and what shape the combined result should be.

blocks.text: 3. Your First GroupBy: Orders by Region
Let's make this concrete with a small orders DataFrame. Seven orders, each one tagged with a region, a product category, a total amount spent, and a quantity of items.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "region":   ["North", "South", "North", "East", "South", "East", "North"],
    "category": ["Electronics", "Clothing", "Clothing", "Electronics", "Electronics", "Clothing", "Electronics"],
    "total":    [250, 80, 120, 300, 150, 60, 400],
    "quantity": [2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1, 4],
})
orders

blocks.text: Now the question: what is the average order total in each region? In plain pandas, selecting the column you care about and calling .mean() after grouping gets you there in one line.

code.content:
orders.groupby("region")["total"].mean()

# region
# East     180.000000
# North    256.666667
# South    115.000000
# Name: total, dtype: float64

blocks.text: Walk through that line using split-apply-combine and it stops feeling like magic. groupby("region") splits the seven rows into three groups: East, North, South. ["total"] narrows each group down to just the total column. .mean() applies the average to each of those three groups independently. Pandas then combines the three averages into the single Series you see printed above, with the region names as the index.

blocks.alt: Your First GroupBy: Orders by Region
blocks.caption: The exact same three steps, applied to a real example.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267412-224722331.png
4. What a GroupBy Object Actually Is

Here is something that trips up almost everyone the first time: calling .groupby() by itself does not actually compute anything. It hands you back a special, somewhat lazy intermediate object, not a table of numbers.

That printed line is not a bug and it is not useful on its own. It is just Python telling you a DataFrameGroupBy object exists somewhere in memory. Pandas has done the split step, remembered which rows belong to which region, and then simply waited. Nothing has been applied or combined yet.

blocks.alt: What a GroupBy Object Actually Is
blocks.caption: A GroupBy object sits there, split but not yet aggregated, until you chain a function onto it.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267412-892953572.png

blocks.title: Printing a raw GroupBy object is a dead end
blocks.content: If your groupby code prints something like <pandas.core.groupby.generic.DataFrameGroupBy object at ...> instead of numbers, that just means you forgot to chain an aggregation onto it. You need to call something like .mean(), .sum(), or .agg() on the grouped object to trigger the apply and combine steps and actually get a result back.

blocks.text: You can reuse that same lazy grouped object for several different aggregations without repeating the groupby call, since the expensive split step already happened once.

code.content:
grouped["total"].sum()

# region
# East     360
# North    770
# South    230
# Name: total, dtype: int64

blocks.title: A gotcha with non-numeric columns
blocks.content: If you call an aggregation on the whole grouped DataFrame instead of picking a column first, like orders.groupby("region").mean(), pandas needs every remaining column to make sense as a number. Text columns such as category get silently dropped in recent pandas versions, or raise an error in older ones. Selecting the column you actually care about first, the way the examples above do, keeps the result predictable.

blocks.text: 5. Grouping by Multiple Columns

Real questions are often more specific than "per region." What about the average order total for each region and product category combination? Pass a list of column names to groupby() instead of a single string and pandas groups by the combination of all of them.

code.content:
orders.groupby(["region", "category"])["total"].mean()

# region  category
# East    Clothing        60.0
#         Electronics    300.0
# North   Clothing       120.0
#         Electronics    325.0
# South   Clothing        80.0
#         Electronics    150.0
# Name: total, dtype: float64

blocks.text: The split step now carves the data into one group per unique region and category pair, instead of one group per region. The result comes back with a hierarchical index, sometimes called a MultiIndex: region on the outer level, category nested underneath it. Reading it top to bottom, every region gets its own block, and inside that block, every category that appears for that region gets its own row.

blocks.caption: Grouping by multiple columns produces one group per unique combination, shown as a hierarchical result.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267412-566887414.png

blocks.title: Group order is sorted by default
blocks.content: groupby sorts the group keys alphabetically or numerically by default, which is why East appears before North and South above even though North was the first region in the raw data. Pass sort=False if you want pandas to leave the group order alone and use the order each group first appears in the data instead.

blocks.text: 6. Common Built-in Aggregations

Once you have a grouped column, pandas gives you a whole set of ready made aggregation methods. They all follow the same shape: split by the group, apply this specific function to each group, combine into a result.
6.1 The Common Ones: Mean, Sum, Count, Min, Max, Std

blocks.content: {"headers":["Method","What it computes"],"rows":[[".mean()","The average value in each group."],[".sum()","The total of all values in each group."],[".count()","How many non-null values are in each group, per column."],[".min()","The smallest value in each group."],[".max()","The largest value in each group."],[".std()","How spread out the values in each group are around the mean."]]}

blocks.text: .std() deserves a plain language explanation since it is less obvious than the rest. A small standard deviation means the values in that group are all bunched close together near the average. A large one means the values are scattered far apart, some way above the mean and some way below it.

code.content:
orders.groupby("region")["total"].mean()
orders.groupby("region")["total"].sum()
orders.groupby("region")["total"].count()
orders.groupby("region")["total"].min()
orders.groupby("region")["total"].max()
orders.groupby("region")["total"].std()

blocks.text: 6.2 Count vs Size: A Common Point of Confusion
.count() and .size() sound like they should do the same thing. They do not, and mixing them up is one of the most common groupby mistakes.

.count() counts non-null values, per column. If a group has five rows but one of them has a missing value in the column you are counting, .count() reports four for that group. .size() counts total rows in the group, full stop, regardless of whether any values are missing. A group with five rows always reports five for .size(), nulls or not.

code.content:
orders_with_nulls = orders.copy()
orders_with_nulls.loc[2, "total"] = None

orders_with_nulls.groupby("region")["total"].count()
# region
# East     2
# North    2
# South    2
# Name: total, dtype: int64

orders_with_nulls.groupby("region").size()
# region
# East     2
# North    3
# South    2
# dtype: int64

blocks.text: Notice North: it still has three rows in the data, so .size() reports 3. But one of those three rows now has a missing total, so .count() on the total column reports only 2. East and South are unaffected since neither of them had a null introduced.

blocks.content: {"headers":["","count()","size()"],"rows":[["What it counts","Non-null values in one specific column","Every row in the group, nulls included"],["Works per column or per group","Per column","Per group as a whole"],["Effect of a missing value","That row is skipped for that column","That row is still counted"]]}

blocks.alt: Count vs Size: A Common Point of Confusion
blocks.caption: The classic gotcha: count skips nulls in a column, size counts every row in the group regardless.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442267412-664995774.png

blocks.title: When to reach for which
blocks.content: Use .size() when the question is "how many rows landed in this group." Use .count() when the question is "how many actual, non-missing values does this specific column have in this group." They agree with each other only when there are no missing values at all.

blocks.text: 7. The agg Method: Multiple Aggregations at Once

Calling .mean(), then .sum(), then .count() as three separate lines works, but it also means pandas redoes the split step three separate times and you end up with three separate results to juggle. .agg() lets you ask for several aggregations in a single call and get one combined result back.
7.1 Applying Several Aggregations to a Column
Pass a list of function names to .agg() and pandas applies every one of them to the same column, then lines the results up side by side as columns in the output.

code.content:
orders.groupby("region")["total"].agg(["mean", "sum", "count"])

#              mean  sum  count
# region
# East        180.0  360      2
# North  256.666667  770      3
# South       115.0  230      2

blocks.text: One split step, three functions applied to each group, one combined table. That is strictly less work than calling .mean(), .sum(), and .count() separately and then trying to merge three Series back together yourself.

blocks.alt: Applying Several Aggregations to a Column
blocks.caption: agg with a list runs several functions on the same column in one pass.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442268180-23897438.png
7.2 Different Aggregations for Different Columns with a Dict

Sometimes different columns need different treatment entirely. You might want the mean of the total column but the sum of the quantity column, in the same call. Pass a dictionary to .agg() instead of a list, mapping each column name to the function you want applied to it.

code.content:
orders.groupby("region").agg({
    "total": "mean",
    "quantity": "sum",
})

#              total  quantity
# region
# East         180.0         2
# North   256.666667         9
# South        115.0         3

blocks.text: The split step is the same as always. The apply step is now different per column: the total column gets averaged, the quantity column gets summed. Pandas combines both into one result table, matched up by region.

blocks.alt: Different Aggregations for Different Columns with a Dict
blocks.caption: agg with a dict lets each column get its own aggregation function.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442268181-303775058.png

blocks.title: Naming your output columns
blocks.content: You can also pass keyword arguments to .agg(), like avg_total=("total", "mean"), to control exactly what the resulting columns get named instead of inheriting the raw function name. This is called named aggregation and it becomes especially handy once you are computing several statistics at once, which the worked example later in this lesson uses.

blocks.text: 8. Iterating Over Groups Directly

Every so often, what you need to do to each group does not fit neatly into a single aggregation function. Maybe you need to print a custom report for every region, or run several unrelated checks on each group's rows. For that, you can loop over a GroupBy object directly. Each step of the loop hands you the group's key and that group's own little DataFrame.

code.content:
for region_name, group_df in orders.groupby("region"):
    print(region_name)
    print(group_df)
    print()

blocks.text: Inside the loop, group_df is a completely normal DataFrame containing only the rows for that one region, so you can do anything with it that you would do with any other DataFrame. If you just want one specific group without looping through all of them, .get_group() gets you straight there.

blocks.title: Treat the loop as an escape hatch, not a default
blocks.content: Looping over groups feels familiar if you are used to writing regular Python loops, but it throws away most of the speed benefit that made groupby worth using in the first place. Most of the time, .agg() or .apply() is a better fit and will run faster. Reach for a plain loop only when the logic genuinely does not reduce to a simple aggregation.

blocks.text: 9. Keeping the Group Column with as_index=False
By default, groupby turns whatever column you grouped by into the index of the result, not a regular column anymore.

code.content:
orders.groupby("region")["total"].mean()
# region is now the index of this Series, not a normal column

blocks.text: Most of the time that is fine. But sometimes you want the result to look and behave like an ordinary, flat DataFrame afterward, for example before merging it with another table or feeding it into a plotting function that expects a plain column. Pass as_index=False to groupby() and the group column stays a regular column instead, with a fresh default integer index put in its place.

code.content:
orders.groupby("region", as_index=False)["total"].mean()

#    region       total
# 0    East  180.000000
# 1   North  256.666667
# 2   South  115.000000

blocks.alt: Keeping the Group Column with as_index=False
blocks.caption: as_index False keeps the grouping column as ordinary data instead of promoting it to the index.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442268182-843415571.png

blocks.title: Why this actually matters
blocks.content: A grouped column trapped in the index cannot be selected with df["region"] the normal way, and it will not show up as a column if you try to merge, filter, or plot the result like a regular table. as_index=False sidesteps all of that by keeping everything as plain columns from the start. .reset_index() after the fact achieves the same thing if you forgot to pass it up front.

blocks.text: 10. Worked Example: Region and Category Together
Let's put everything from this lesson together in one call: grouping by two columns at once, computing several different statistics, and keeping the result as a flat, easy to read DataFrame.

code.content:
summary = orders.groupby(["region", "category"], as_index=False).agg(
    avg_total=("total", "mean"),
    total_revenue=("total", "sum"),
    order_count=("total", "count"),
    total_units=("quantity", "sum"),
)
summary

blocks.text: Read that line the same way you have been reading every groupby call in this lesson. Split: one group per unique region and category combination. Apply: four different statistics computed independently for each of those groups, the average and sum and count of total, plus the sum of quantity. Combine: one flat table, thanks to as_index=False, with clearly named columns instead of a raw MultiIndex mess.

Every one of those six rows answers a real business question in one glance: North Electronics is both the busiest combination, with two separate orders, and the biggest revenue driver, with 650 in total sales. That kind of table is exactly what you would hand to someone building a dashboard, and it came from a single chained groupby call.
If you skip named aggregation and use the dict form from earlier instead, you get a result with multi level columns, which you can flatten by joining the level names together yourself.

code.content:
grouped_stats = orders.groupby(["region", "category"]).agg({"total": ["mean", "sum"]})
grouped_stats.columns = ["_".join(col) for col in grouped_stats.columns]
grouped_stats = grouped_stats.reset_index()

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Region and Category Together
blocks.caption: The full pipeline: split by two columns, apply several aggregations, combine into one flat table.
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442268182-740437526.png
11. Quick Recap

items: Every groupby call is split, apply, combine, whether you see those three words in the code or not.
A GroupBy object by itself is lazy and uncomputed. Chain an aggregation like .mean() or .sum() onto it to actually get a result.
Pass a list of columns to groupby() to group by a combination of values, which produces a hierarchical result.
count() counts non-null values per column. size() counts every row in the group, nulls included. They only agree when there is no missing data.
agg() lets you run several aggregations at once, either a list applied to one column or a dict applied differently across several columns.
A for loop over a GroupBy object is a real escape hatch for custom logic, but agg() or apply() is almost always the faster, cleaner choice.
as_index=False keeps the grouping columns as regular data instead of turning them into the index, which matters when you want a flat DataFrame afterward.

blocks.text: groupby is the tool you will use more than almost anything else in pandas once you start working with real, messy, multi column data. Get comfortable with split-apply-combine as your mental model, and every variation you run into after this, agg, transform, filter, apply, will feel like a small twist on something you already understand rather than a brand new thing to memorize.
